flags.sentence: Anvil pruners are fine for clearing dead wood only.
flags.suggestion: Use bypass (scissor-action) pruners. Anvil pruners, which crush the stem against a flat edge, are fine for clearing dead wood only.

flags.sentence: One source says to remove no more than about a third of a plant's crown in any one year.
flags.suggestion: One source says to remove no more than about a third of the plant's top growth in any one year.

flags.sentence: Some rose sources renovate an old rose in one go instead of in stages.
flags.problem: 1: about the sources, not the plant
flags.suggestion: An old rose can also be renovated in one go instead of in stages.

flags.sentence: Rose sources disagree on what to call cutting back by a third: some call it "light" pruning, and another calls it "moderate".
flags.problem: 3: a naming quarrel a gardener cannot act on
flags.suggestion: Cutting back by a third may be called light or moderate pruning; either way it is the same amount.

flags.sentence: so the rose can form hips and slow down for winter
flags.suggestion: Stop in early-to-mid autumn, so the rose can form hips (the round seed pods) and slow down for winter.

flags.sentence: This care advice comes mainly from UK and US gardening services.
flags.suggestion: Timings and amounts may differ where you live.

flags.sentence: Pay closer attention to watering a newly planted rose.
flags.suggestion: Say what to do (how often or how much), or drop it.

flags.sentence: Most sources leave a newly planted rose unpruned, apart from dead wood, until it has established; two prune at planting or in the first winter.
flags.problem: 1: counts sources instead of telling the gardener
flags.suggestion: Usually a newly planted rose is left unpruned, apart from dead wood, until it has established; a couple of sources prune at planting or in the first winter.

flags.sentence: This care advice comes mainly from UK and US gardening services.
flags.suggestion: Timings and amounts may differ where you live.

flags.sentence: covering the graft union
flags.suggestion: covering the graft union (the knobbly joint near the base where the rose was grafted onto its roots)

flags.sentence: One source also builds a collar of tar paper or wire mesh around the rose and fills it with straw, pine bark or peat moss.
flags.problem: 1: reads as what a source does
flags.suggestion: You can also build a collar of tar paper or wire mesh around the rose and fill it with straw, pine bark or peat moss.

flags.sentence: This care advice comes mainly from US gardening services.
flags.suggestion: Timings and amounts may differ where you live.

flags.sentence: My approach to a heavy renovation is to spread it over two or three years, about a third at a time. Some sources do it all in one go, and I couldn't find a rule for roses on which to choose.
flags.problem: 1/6: about my search and the sources
flags.suggestion: For a heavy renovation, spread it over two or three years, about a third at a time. Doing it all in one go also works; there is no rule for roses on which to choose.

flags.sentence: I couldn't find signs, or a waiting time, for judging whether a hard-pruned rose is recovering.
flags.problem: 1: about the search, not the plant
flags.suggestion: There are no set signs or waiting time for judging recovery. If no new growth appears during the growing season, ask your local rose society.

flags.sentence: I can't tell you which reason applies to your rose. Here are the reasons sources give, with what to look for and what they suggest.
flags.suggestion: Any of these could be the reason. Check each one against your rose.

flags.sentence: My care tips give the feeding pattern.
flags.problem: 3: points elsewhere without saying what to do
flags.suggestion: Feed in spring and through summer, stopping by mid-to-late summer.

flags.sentence: I couldn't find how much pruning is too much; a local rose society can help.
flags.suggestion: How much pruning is too much isn't known; a local rose society can help.

flags.sentence: Sources link spotted petals with grey fuzz to grey mould (botrytis), which is more common in cool, wet weather.
flags.suggestion: Spotted petals with grey fuzz point to grey mould (botrytis), which is more common in cool, wet weather.

flags.sentence: Sources link brown or white streaks on petals, or distorted flowers, to thrips.
flags.problem: 1: about the sources; thrips not explained
flags.suggestion: Brown or white streaks on petals, or distorted flowers, point to thrips (tiny sap-sucking insects).

flags.sentence: Sources link holes in buds, with caterpillars, to budworm.
flags.suggestion: Holes in buds, with caterpillars present, point to budworm (a caterpillar that eats buds).

flags.sentence: The shoot and its leaves can look perfectly healthy; what's missing is a flower bud at the tip.
flags.suggestion: The shoot and its leaves can look perfectly healthy.

flags.sentence: The cause of blind shoots isn't known.
flags.problem: 3: nothing to act on in this step
flags.suggestion: Drop it here (it is covered in the flowering answer).

flags.sentence: Look again at the tip on the plant, not in a photo.
flags.suggestion: That's alright. Take another look at the tip when you can.

flags.sentence: Remove only the wood you are sure is dead, damaged or diseased.
flags.suggestion: Remove only the wood you are sure is bad. Heavy pruning of healthy canes at this stage can reduce flowering.

flags.sentence: Go gently and avoid damaging the new leaves.
flags.suggestion: Work carefully around new leaves, which tear easily.

flags.sentence: For anything that looks like canker or disease
flags.suggestion: For anything that looks like canker (sunken, discoloured patches on the cane) or other disease, cut well below the affected part, and bin the prunings or burn them where local rules allow.

flags.sentence: Don't rely on "Ht" or "Fl" in a rose's name to tell you its type: one New Zealand shop sells a rose as "Ht" that its own page describes as a Floribunda.
flags.problem: 1/4: leans on a shop example; abbreviations not explained
flags.suggestion: "Ht" (Hybrid Tea) or "Fl" (Floribunda) in a rose's name doesn't reliably tell you its type; one shop sells a rose as "Ht" that it describes as a Floribunda.

flags.sentence: At least one New Zealand nursery calls a shrub rose a "bush" rose.
flags.suggestion: "Bush" on a label doesn't always say which type a rose is; shrub roses are sometimes sold as "bush" roses.

overall: Mostly plain and actionable, but several lines talk about what sources or the app found rather than the plant, a few terms (crown, hips, graft union, canker, thrips, Ht/Fl) go unexplained, and a few lines are empty or repeat each other.
